cards.meaning: JavaScript objects form a prototype chain. When you read a property that is not an own property, the engine walks that object's internal [[Prototype]] link, then that object's prototype, and so on, until it finds the property or reaches null. There is no separate class-instance runtime underneath ES6 class.

cards.front: How do you read [[Prototype]], and where does the chain end?
cards.meaning: Prefer Object.getPrototypeOf(obj). __proto__ is a legacy accessor on Object.prototype — avoid it in new code, but recognize it in interviews. A plain object's [[Prototype]] is Object.prototype; Object.getPrototypeOf(Object.prototype) === null.

cards.front: Property miss vs assignment vs delete on the chain?
cards.meaning: A get walks [[Prototype]] until a hit or null → undefined. Assignment usually creates an own property (shadowing), not mutating the prototype. delete removes the own property so lookup walks again and can find the prototype value.
cards.example: obj.kind = 'dog' shadows proto.kind; delete obj.kind; obj.kind // 'animal'

cards.meaning: A new object whose [[Prototype]] is proto (or null). Misses delegate to proto. Object.create(null) is a dictionary with no Object.prototype — no inherited toString/hasOwnProperty.
cards.example: const dog = Object.create(animal); dog.speak(); // via animal.  dict.toString // undefined

cards.meaning: Create empty object; set its [[Prototype]] to Ctor.prototype; call Ctor with this = new object; return that object unless the constructor returns another object (primitives ignored).
A returned object replaces the default new instance. A returned primitive is ignored; you still get the instance with own fields from this.
cards.example:
function Weird() { this.a = 1; return { b: 2 }; } new Weird(); // { b: 2 }
function Normal() { this.a = 1; return 5; } new Normal(); // { a: 1 }

cards.meaning: Animal.prototype is the object instances link to via new. getPrototypeOf(dog) is dog's actual [[Prototype]] (usually Animal.prototype). dog.prototype is usually undefined — instances aren't constructors. Animal.prototype.constructor === Animal by default; repair it after replacing Dog.prototype.

cards.front: Call a function constructor as a plain function (no new)?
cards.meaning: Uses default this binding: in strict mode this.name = ... throws; in sloppy mode it can create or pollute globals. class constructors instead throw TypeError without new.

cards.front: What does obj instanceof Ctor check?
cards.meaning: Whether Ctor.prototype appears anywhere on obj's prototype chain — not exclusive construction history. Manual setPrototypeOf/Object.create, cross-realm objects (iframe Array.prototype), and Symbol.hasInstance can surprise.
cards.example: dog instanceof Animal; // true  dog instanceof Object; // true  dog instanceof Array; // false

cards.front: Own vs inherited: Object.hasOwn vs in?
cards.meaning: Object.hasOwn (preferred) / hasOwnProperty are true for own data (name) and false for prototype methods (speak). The in operator sees inherited properties too: 'speak' in dog → true.

ES6 class is syntax over constructor + prototype with real differences: always-strict body; TDZ like let (new Person() before class Person {} → ReferenceError); TypeError if called without new; prototype methods are non-enumerable. Still: methods on Ctor.prototype, own data from constructor/fields.
cards.example:
class A {} A(); // TypeError
const x = new Person(); class Person {} // ReferenceError

cards.front: Class field count vs method inc() — where stored? a.inc === b.inc?
cards.meaning: count is an own property per instance. inc lives on Counter.prototype — one shared function, so a.inc === b.inc. a.count and b.count are different own slots: after a.count = 5, b.count is still 0.

cards.front: Prototype method vs arrow class field?
cards.meaning: Method on Ctor.prototype — one shared function, this from call site. Arrow instance field — own property per instance, lexical this to the instance at construction; extra allocation per instance, stable detached callbacks (avoids .bind() for older React class handlers).

cards.front: extends / super mechanically — and this before super()?
cards.meaning: Dog.prototype's [[Prototype]] is Animal.prototype; Dog's [[Prototype]] is Animal (statics). super() in a subclass constructor runs the parent constructor and must run before using this. super.method() looks up the parent prototype chain, not a dynamic caller.
cards.example: class Dog extends Animal { constructor(name, breed) { super(name); this.breed = breed; } }

cards.meaning: Object.create(Animal.prototype), then repair Dog.prototype.constructor = Dog. Pre-class Animal.call(this, name) is like super() for own fields. Wrong: Dog.prototype = Animal.prototype (shared one object; methods overwrite each other).

cards.front: Where do class statics live, and how do they inherit?
cards.meaning: On the constructor function itself (User.createGuest(), not on an instance). With extends, Object.getPrototypeOf(Dog) === Animal so statics follow the constructor chain; Object.getPrototypeOf(Dog.prototype) === Animal.prototype is the instance method chain.
cards.example: class User { static createGuest() { return new User('guest'); } } User.createGuest();

cards.front: Prototypes vs this — what question does each answer?
cards.meaning: Prototypes answer where the function is found; this answers which receiver was used when calling it. this inside prototype methods still follows call-site rules.
